notes.h: The International Standard Atmosphere and airspeeds
notes.body:
Aircraft performance depends on air pressure, density and temperature, which vary with altitude and weather. The International Standard Atmosphere (ISA), defined by ICAO, gives a common reference.

ISA sea-level values: T0 = 288.15 K (15 °C), p0 = 101 325 Pa, ρ0 = 1.225 kg/m³, a0 = 340.3 m/s and μ0 = 1.789 × 10⁻⁵ Pa·s.

The model rests on two laws:
- Hydrostatic equation: dp/dh = −ρg.
- Ideal gas law: p = ρRT, with R = 287.05 J/(kg·K) and γ = 1.4 for air.

Layers:
- Troposphere (0–11 km): temperature falls linearly at 6.5 K/km, T = T0 − 0.0065h. Integrating gives p/p0 = (T/T0)^5.256 and ρ/ρ0 = (T/T0)^4.256.
- Lower stratosphere (11–20 km): isothermal at 216.65 K, so pressure decays exponentially, p = p11·exp[−g(h − 11 000)/(RT)].
- At 11 km: p = 22.63 kPa, ρ = 0.364 kg/m³, a = 295.1 m/s.

Speed of sound: a = √(γRT). It depends on temperature only, so it is constant through the isothermal layer. The density ratio is σ = ρ/ρ0.

Airspeeds:
- IAS is read from the airspeed indicator.
- CAS is IAS corrected for instrument and position error.
- EAS is CAS corrected for compressibility. It gives the true dynamic pressure, q = ½ρV² = ½ρ0·VE².
- TAS is the speed relative to the air: VE = V√σ.
- Loads, stalling and handling depend on EAS. Navigation, Mach number and kinetic energy depend on TAS.

Altimetry: an altimeter is a barometer calibrated to ISA.
- Set to 1013.25 hPa, it shows pressure altitude, which is the basis of flight levels.
- QNH gives altitude above mean sea level; QFE gives height above the aerodrome.
- Density altitude is the ISA altitude with the same density as the actual air. On a hot day it is higher than pressure altitude, so engines and wings perform worse and take-off runs lengthen.

Worked example: an aircraft flies at 8000 m in ISA at 220 m/s TAS.
- T = 288.15 − 52 = 236.15 K.
- p = 101 325 × (236.15/288.15)^5.256 = 35.6 kPa, so ρ = p/(RT) = 0.525 kg/m³ and σ = 0.429.
- a = √(1.4 × 287.05 × 236.15) = 308.1 m/s, so M = 0.71.
- EAS = 220 × √0.429 = 144 m/s, and q = 12.7 kPa.

Common exam pitfalls:
- Using °C instead of kelvin in p = ρRT or a = √(γRT).
- Applying the tropospheric power law above 11 km.
- Confusing EAS and TAS, for example by putting TAS with ρ0 into ½ρV².
- Forgetting that the speed of sound falls with temperature, not with pressure.

An aerofoil section is described by its chord c, camber line, thickness distribution and angle of attack α. Per unit span:
- Lift: L' = ½ρV²·c·cl.
- Drag: D' = ½ρV²·c·cd.
- Pitching moment: M' = ½ρV²·c²·cm.
- The pressure coefficient is Cp = (p − p∞)/(½ρV²). It is negative over most of the upper surface at positive lift.

Lift arises because the aerofoil turns the flow downward, with lower pressure above and higher below. In potential flow, the Kutta condition requires flow to leave the sharp trailing edge smoothly. That condition fixes a unique circulation Γ, and the Kutta–Joukowski theorem gives L' = ρ∞·V∞·Γ. Inviscid theory predicts zero drag (d'Alembert's paradox), so drag comes from viscosity.

Thin aerofoil theory (Glauert, 1926):
- cl = 2π(α − αL0), α in radians: about 0.11 per degree (real sections roughly 0.10).
- A symmetric section has αL0 = 0. Positive camber makes αL0 negative, so the section lifts at zero incidence.
- The aerodynamic centre, where cm does not change with α, is at the quarter chord. For a symmetric section, cm,ac = 0.
- The centre of pressure moves with α on a cambered section.

Boundary layers (Prandtl, 1904): viscous effects are confined to a thin layer next to the surface.
- The Reynolds number Re = ρVc/μ controls behaviour (a few million for a light aircraft wing).
- A laminar boundary layer has low skin friction but separates easily. A turbulent layer has higher skin friction but more near-wall momentum, so it resists separation in an adverse pressure gradient.
- Flat-plate skin friction coefficients: laminar (Blasius) Cf = 1.328/√Re; turbulent approximately Cf = 0.074/Re^(1/5).
- Profile drag = skin friction + pressure (form) drag.

Stall: as α increases, the adverse pressure gradient on the upper surface steepens until the boundary layer separates. Lift then collapses and drag rises; typical clmax is 1.2–1.6. High-lift devices raise CLmax: trailing-edge flaps add camber and area, and leading-edge slats and slots re-energise the boundary layer. Vortex generators delay separation by mixing.

Worked example: a symmetric section with c = 1.5 m at α = 6° flies at 50 m/s at sea level.
- cl = 2π × 0.1047 = 0.658.
- q = ½ × 1.225 × 50² = 1531 Pa, so L' = 1531 × 1.5 × 0.658 = 1.51 kN/m.
- Re = 1.225 × 50 × 1.5/1.789 × 10⁻⁵ = 5.1 × 10⁶.

Common exam pitfalls:
- Using degrees in cl = 2πα.
- Confusing section cl with whole-wing CL.
- Placing the aerodynamic centre at the centre of pressure.
- Assuming a turbulent boundary layer always means more drag. On bluff bodies, delayed separation can reduce total drag.

notes.h: Finite wings, lifting-line theory and induced drag
notes.body:
Wing geometry: span b, area S, aspect ratio AR = b²/S, taper ratio λ = ctip/croot and sweep Λ.

On a finite wing, higher pressure below the wing spills around the tips towards the lower pressure above. This forms tip vortices and a trailing vortex sheet. The sheet induces downwash w at the wing, which reduces the effective angle of attack by αi and tilts the local lift vector backwards. The rearward component is induced drag.

Prandtl's lifting-line theory (1918–19):
- An elliptic spanwise lift distribution gives uniform downwash, with αi = CL/(πAR), and the minimum possible induced drag, CDi = CL²/(πAR).
- For other distributions, CDi = CL²/(πeAR), where the span efficiency factor e ≤ 1.
- In a whole-aircraft drag polar, the Oswald factor e (typically 0.7–0.85) also absorbs the lift-dependent part of profile drag.
- The lift-curve slope falls with aspect ratio: a = a0/[1 + a0/(πAR)] for elliptic loading. With a0 = 2π, AR = 6 gives 4.71/rad and AR = 10 gives 5.24/rad.

In dimensional form, Di = W²/(½ρV²·π·b²·e). Induced drag therefore depends on span loading W/b, not on aspect ratio as such. It falls with the square of speed, so it dominates at low speed, in the climb and in the approach. Zero-lift (parasite) drag rises with V². Total drag is a minimum where CDi = CD0.

Drag polar: CD = CD0 + k·CL², with k = 1/(πeAR).
- Minimum drag occurs at CL* = √(CD0/k).
- (L/D)max = 1/(2√(k·CD0)). It rises with span and with low CD0, which is why gliders have very high aspect ratios.

Getting close to elliptic loading:
- An elliptic planform, as on the Spitfire.
- A straight taper of about 0.4–0.5 with modest twist.
- Washout, which twists the tips nose-down. It also makes the root stall first, so the ailerons stay effective.

Winglets and raked tips cut induced drag at the cost of extra root bending moment. Ground effect also reduces it.

Worked example: W = 50 kN, S = 30 m², e = 0.85, V = 50 m/s at sea level, so q = 1531 Pa and CL = 1.09.
- AR = 6 (b = 13.4 m): CDi = 1.09²/(π × 0.85 × 6) = 0.0739, giving Di = 3.40 kN.
- AR = 10 (b = 17.3 m): CDi = 0.0444, giving Di = 2.04 kN, which is 40% less.

Common exam pitfalls:
- Assuming induced drag rises with speed.
- Confusing the span efficiency factor with the Oswald factor.
- Forgetting that higher AR raises wing weight and root bending moment.
- Treating sweep as a way to reduce induced drag. It exists to delay compressibility effects.

The Mach number is M = V/a. Below about M = 0.3, density changes are under 5% and incompressible methods work. Flight regimes are roughly subsonic (M < 0.8), transonic (0.8–1.2), supersonic and hypersonic (M > 5).

Isentropic stagnation relations (γ = 1.4):
- T0/T = 1 + ½(γ − 1)M² = 1 + 0.2M².
- p0/p = (T0/T)^(γ/(γ−1)) = (T0/T)^3.5.
- ρ0/ρ = (T0/T)^(1/(γ−1)) = (T0/T)^2.5.
- At M = 0.8, T0/T = 1.128 and p0/p = 1.524. Incompressible Bernoulli underestimates this rise.

Subsonic compressibility: the Prandtl–Glauert rule, Cp = Cp0/√(1 − M∞²), scales low-speed pressure coefficients. It fails as M approaches 1.

Transonic effects:
- The critical Mach number is the freestream M at which sonic flow first appears on the surface. Beyond it, a shock forms on the upper surface. Drag divergence follows, and shock-induced separation can cause buffet.
- Remedies: sweep, reducing the normal Mach component to M·cos Λ (Busemann, 1935); thinner sections; supercritical aerofoils (Whitcomb); and area ruling.

Normal shock waves: flow passes from supersonic to subsonic in a very thin region. Pressure, density and temperature rise, and stagnation pressure falls as entropy rises.
- M2² = [1 + 0.2M1²]/[1.4M1² − 0.2].
- p2/p1 = 1 + (2γ/(γ + 1))(M1² − 1).
- For M1 = 2: M2 = 0.577, p2/p1 = 4.5, ρ2/ρ1 = 2.67, T2/T1 = 1.69 and p02/p01 = 0.721.
- Oblique shocks and expansion fans turn supersonic flow. Weak disturbances travel along Mach lines at μ = arcsin(1/M), which is 30° at M = 2.
- A pitot tube in supersonic flow reads the stagnation pressure behind a normal shock (the Rayleigh pitot formula), not the free-stream value.

Nozzles: the area–velocity relation dA/A = (M² − 1)dV/V shows that subsonic flow speeds up in a converging duct and supersonic flow in a diverging one.
- A convergent–divergent nozzle reaches M = 1 at the throat, where it chokes. The critical pressure ratio is p*/p0 = 0.528.
- The exit Mach number follows from the area ratio, A/A* = (1/M)[(2/(γ + 1))(1 + 0.2M²)]³. For example, A/A* = 1.6875 for M = 2.
- Choked mass flow is ṁ = 0.0404·A*·p0/√T0 (SI units, air).

Worked example: at 11 km (T = 216.65 K) and M = 0.85, the total temperature is 216.65 × (1 + 0.2 × 0.7225) = 248.0 K. A temperature probe reads close to this.

Common exam pitfalls:
- Using incompressible Bernoulli above M ≈ 0.3.
- Mixing static and stagnation conditions.
- Using downstream values in the shock relations.
- Applying Prandtl–Glauert near M = 1.
- Thinking a shock conserves stagnation pressure. It conserves stagnation temperature (adiabatic) but not p0.

notes.h: Thrust, propulsive efficiency and engine types
notes.body:
All air-breathing engines produce thrust by accelerating air rearwards. The momentum equation gives F = ṁ(Ve − V0) + (pe − pa)Ae, neglecting fuel mass. The second term is pressure thrust for a jet that is not fully expanded.

Efficiencies:
- Propulsive efficiency ηp = useful thrust power/(rate of kinetic energy added to the air) = 2/(1 + Ve/V0). It is high when a large mass flow is given a small velocity increase.
- Ideal Brayton thermal efficiency depends only on pressure ratio: ηth = 1 − 1/rp^((γ−1)/γ), giving 0.48 at rp = 10, 0.60 at 25 and 0.65 at 40. Real cycles are limited by losses and turbine entry temperature.
- Overall efficiency η0 = ηth × ηp = thrust power/fuel energy rate.
- Thrust-specific fuel consumption (TSFC) is fuel mass flow per unit thrust, e.g. kg/(N·h). Lower is better.

Engine types:
- Turbojet: all air passes through the core. Its high jet velocity suits supersonic flight but is inefficient and noisy at subsonic speed.
- Turbofan: a large fan drives bypass air around the core. Modern civil engines have bypass ratios of about 10 or more, and geared fans let the fan turn slower than the low-pressure turbine. This gives high ηp, low noise and low TSFC, at the cost of a large, heavy nacelle and ground clearance problems.
- Turboprop: the core drives a propeller through a gearbox. It is very efficient below about M 0.6, beyond which propeller tip compressibility limits it. Thrust power = ηprop × shaft power.
- Ramjet and scramjet: ram compression only, so they need high flight speed.
- Rocket: carries its own oxidiser and is independent of air. The Tsiolkovsky equation (1903) gives Δv = ve·ln(m0/mf), with specific impulse Isp = ve/g0.

Decarbonisation: sustainable aviation fuels are largely drop-in for kerosene. Hydrogen has high energy per kilogram but low energy per volume, needing large cryogenic tanks.

Worked example: two engines each give 20 kN at V0 = 200 m/s.
- Engine A: ṁ = 50 kg/s with Ve = 600 m/s. ηp = 2/(1 + 3) = 0.50, and wasted jet kinetic energy is ½ × 50 × 400² = 4 MW.
- Engine B: ṁ = 200 kg/s with Ve = 300 m/s. ηp = 2/(1 + 1.5) = 0.80, and wasted kinetic energy is only 1 MW.
- Both deliver 4 MW of thrust power; B needs far less fuel.

Common exam pitfalls:
- Confusing thrust (N) with thrust power (W).
- Leaving out pressure thrust for an under-expanded or over-expanded nozzle.
- Writing ηp in terms of the wrong velocity ratio.
- Assuming a higher jet velocity is always better; it lowers propulsive efficiency.

notes.h: Level flight, climb, turn, range and endurance
notes.body:
In steady level flight L = W and T = D, with drag polar CD = CD0 + k·CL².

Stall and turning:
- Stall speed: Vs = √(2W/(ρ·S·CLmax)).
- Load factor in a level turn: n = L/W = 1/cos φ for bank angle φ. Stall speed rises as √n, so a 60° bank (n = 2) raises it by 41%.
- Turn radius r = V²/(g·tan φ); turn rate ω = g·tan φ/V.

Drag and speed:
- Zero-lift drag rises with V² and induced drag falls with 1/V². Their sum is a minimum at the minimum drag speed VMD, where CL = CL* = √(CD0/k) and L/D is maximum.
- For jets, thrust is roughly independent of speed. Maximum endurance is at VMD. Maximum range, which maximises V/D, is at 3^(1/4)·VMD = 1.316 VMD.
- For propeller aircraft, power matters, so maximum endurance is at the minimum power speed VMP ≈ 0.76 VMD and maximum range is at VMD.
- Below VMD (the back of the drag curve), slowing down needs more thrust, so speed is unstable.

Climb and glide:
- sin γ = (T − D)/W. Rate of climb ROC = V·sin γ = (T − D)V/W, the excess power per unit weight.
- Gliding with no thrust: tan γ = D/L, so still-air glide distance = height × (L/D). Best glide is at VMD.

Breguet range and endurance (cruise-climb at constant L/D):
- Jet: R = (V/c)(L/D)·ln(W0/W1) and E = (1/c)(L/D)·ln(W0/W1), with c the TSFC expressed per second (weight of fuel per unit thrust per second).
- Propeller: R = (ηp/c')(L/D)·ln(W0/W1), with c' the power-specific fuel consumption converted to units of 1/m.
- Range improves with high L/D, low c and low empty weight (high W0/W1).

Field lengths grow with weight, density altitude, tailwind and runway slope; flaps cut lift-off speed at some drag cost.

Worked example: a light aircraft of mass 1100 kg has S = 16.2 m² and CLmax = 1.5.
- W = 10.8 kN, so Vs = √(2 × 10 791/(1.225 × 16.2 × 1.5)) = 26.9 m/s at sea level.
- In a 45° banked turn, n = 1.41 and Vs = 32.0 m/s.
- At 45 m/s and 45° bank, r = 45²/9.81 = 206 m and ω = 0.218 rad/s = 12.5°/s.

Common exam pitfalls:
- Using mass instead of weight.
- Leaving TSFC in per-hour units inside the Breguet equation.
- Mixing EAS and TAS in range calculations.
- Assuming best range speed is the same for jets and propeller aircraft.
- Forgetting that the logarithmic weight ratio uses initial over final weight.

notes.h: Static stability, dynamic modes and flight controls
notes.body:
Static stability is the initial tendency to return towards trim after a disturbance. Dynamic stability is whether the motion that follows dies away. A statically stable aircraft can still be dynamically unstable.

Longitudinal static stability:
- It needs dCm/dα < 0 about the centre of gravity (CG), giving a restoring moment, and Cm0 > 0 to trim at positive lift.
- The neutral point (NP) is the CG position at which dCm/dα = 0.
- Static margin Kn = hn − h (fractions of mean aerodynamic chord c̄) must be positive, so the CG lies ahead of the NP; typically 5–20%.
- Simplified stick-fixed neutral point: hn = h0 + V̄H·(at/a)·(1 − dε/dα). Here h0 is the wing–body aerodynamic centre, V̄H = St·lt/(S·c̄) the tail volume coefficient and dε/dα the downwash gradient.
- The aft CG limit is set by the minimum static margin; the forward limit by elevator power to trim and flare, and by stick forces.

Lateral–directional static stability:
- Directional (weathercock) stability needs Cnβ > 0, provided mainly by the fin.
- The dihedral effect needs Clβ < 0, so a sideslip produces a roll away from it. It comes from dihedral, a high wing position and sweepback.

Dynamic modes:
- Longitudinal short period: rapid, heavily damped pitch oscillation lasting a few seconds.
- Phugoid: a slow exchange of height and speed at nearly constant angle of attack, lightly damped. Lanchester's approximation gives its period as T ≈ π√2·V/g, about 45 s at 100 m/s.
- Roll subsidence: fast, non-oscillatory.
- Spiral mode: slow and often mildly divergent. Strong directional stability with weak dihedral effect makes it worse.
- Dutch roll: a coupled yaw–roll oscillation. Strong dihedral effect with weak directional stability makes it worse, so swept-wing jets use yaw dampers.

Controls:
- Elevator for pitch, ailerons for roll and rudder for yaw. Aileron deflection causes adverse yaw, reduced by differential or Frise ailerons.
- Fly-by-wire allows relaxed static stability, cutting trim drag and adding agility, with computers supplying artificial stability.

Worked example: h0 = 0.25, V̄H = 0.6, at = 3.5/rad, a = 5.0/rad and dε/dα = 0.4.
- hn = 0.25 + 0.6 × 0.7 × 0.6 = 0.502.
- With the CG at 0.30c̄, Kn = 0.20.
- For a 5% minimum margin, the aft CG limit is 0.452c̄.

Common exam pitfalls:
- Sign errors. Stability needs a negative Cmα but a positive Cnβ.
- Confusing the aerodynamic centre of the wing with the neutral point of the aircraft.
- Assuming that more dihedral is always better, given its effect on Dutch roll.

Loads and load factors:
- Load factor n = L/W. Limit load, the largest expected in service, must cause no permanent deformation. Ultimate load = 1.5 × limit (CS/FAR 25.303) and must be carried without failure for at least 3 seconds (CS/FAR 25.305).
- For large aeroplanes (CS-25), the positive limit manoeuvring load factor is n = 2.1 + 24 000/(W + 10 000), with W in lb. It must be at least 2.5 and need not exceed 3.8. The negative limit is −1.0 up to VC, falling linearly to zero at VD.
- The V–n diagram is bounded by the stall curve n = (V/Vs)², the limit load factors and the dive speed VD. The manoeuvre speed VA = Vs√nmax is where they meet.
- Sharp-edged gust: Δn = ρ0·VE·a·U/(2W/S), so lightly loaded wings respond more. Certification uses alleviation factors and tuned gusts.

Construction is semi-monocoque: skins stiffened by internal members.
- Wing box: spar caps carry most of the bending, spar webs carry vertical shear, and skins with stringers carry bending and torsion (as shear flow). Ribs maintain the profile, spread concentrated loads and limit the buckling length of panels.
- Fuselage: frames, stringers and skin. Pressurisation causes hoop stress σh = pr/t and longitudinal stress σl = pr/(2t).
- Thin-walled closed sections in torsion follow the Bredt–Batho result, q = T/(2A), where A is the area enclosed by the wall mid-line. The twist rate is dθ/dz = T·∮ds/t/(4A²G).
- Thin compression panels buckle at σcr = k·π²E/[12(1 − ν²)]·(t/b)².

Materials:
- 2024 aluminium (damage tolerant) for the fuselage and tension-loaded lower wing skins; 7075 (stronger) for compression-loaded upper skins.
- Titanium for hot or highly loaded parts; carbon fibre composites make up about half the structural weight of the Boeing 787 and Airbus A350.

Fatigue and design philosophy:
- Safe-life parts are retired after a set life. Fail-safe structures have alternative load paths.
- Damage-tolerant design assumes cracks exist and sets inspection intervals so that they are found before they reach critical length.
- The Comet 1 losses of 1954, traced to fatigue cracking at fuselage cut-out corners, and the Aloha Airlines Flight 243 failure of 1988 (multiple-site damage) shaped these rules.

Worked example: a cabin with differential pressure 58 kPa has radius 1.95 m and skin 1.8 mm thick.
- σh = 58 000 × 1.95/0.0018 = 62.8 MPa.
- σl = 31.4 MPa.
- These are low against static strength, but the cycle repeats every flight, so fatigue governs.

Common exam pitfalls:
- Confusing limit and ultimate load.
- Using the diameter instead of the radius in pr/t.
- Using the outer rather than the mid-line enclosed area in q = T/(2A).

cards.f: State the ISA sea-level temperature, pressure and density.
What is the ISA temperature lapse rate in the troposphere and where does it end?
cards.b: 6.5 K per km, from sea level up to the tropopause at 11 km. Above that the ISA is isothermal at 216.65 K up to 20 km.

cards.f: Write the hydrostatic equation and the ideal gas law.
cards.b: dp/dh = −ρg and p = ρRT, with R = 287.05 J/(kg·K) for air. Combining them with a temperature profile gives the ISA pressure variation.

cards.f: Give the ISA pressure ratio in the troposphere.
cards.b: p/p0 = (T/T0)^(g/(LR)) = (T/T0)^5.256, with L = 0.0065 K/m. The density ratio uses exponent 4.256.

cards.f: Why is the speed of sound constant between 11 and 20 km in the ISA?
cards.b: Because a = √(γRT) depends only on temperature, which is constant at 216.65 K there. Its value is about 295 m/s.

cards.f: Relate equivalent airspeed and true airspeed.
cards.b: VE = V√σ, where σ = ρ/ρ0. EAS gives the same dynamic pressure at sea-level density as TAS gives at the actual density.

cards.f: Why are structural loads and stalling speeds quoted in EAS?
cards.b: Aerodynamic forces depend on dynamic pressure ½ρV² = ½ρ0VE². A given EAS gives the same forces at any altitude, while the TAS for those forces rises with height.

cards.f: What does an altimeter set to 1013.25 hPa display?
cards.b: Pressure altitude: the ISA altitude at which the measured static pressure occurs. It is the basis of flight levels, so all aircraft share a common reference.

cards.f: What is density altitude and why does it matter?
cards.b: The ISA altitude with the same air density as the actual conditions. Hot, high or humid days raise density altitude, reducing engine power, propeller thrust and lift, and lengthening take-off distances.

cards.f: Calculate the ISA temperature, pressure and density at 11 km.
Define the pressure coefficient.
cards.b: Cp = (p − p∞)/(½ρ∞V∞²). Cp = 1 at a stagnation point, and negative values show suction.

cards.f: State the Kutta–Joukowski theorem.
cards.b: Lift per unit span equals ρ∞V∞Γ, where Γ is the circulation around the aerofoil. The Kutta condition fixes Γ by requiring smooth flow off the sharp trailing edge.

cards.f: What lift-curve slope does thin aerofoil theory predict?
cards.b: dcl/dα = 2π per radian (about 0.11 per degree), with cl = 2π(α − αL0).

cards.f: Where is the aerodynamic centre of a thin aerofoil and why is it useful?
cards.b: At the quarter chord. The pitching moment about it does not change with angle of attack, so it is a fixed reference for stability, unlike the moving centre of pressure.

cards.f: What is the effect of positive camber on the lift curve?
cards.b: It shifts the curve to the left, making αL0 negative, so the section lifts at zero incidence. It also gives a negative (nose-down) cm,ac. The slope stays about 2π.

cards.f: Distinguish skin friction drag from pressure (form) drag.
cards.b: Skin friction is the tangential viscous shear on the surface. Pressure drag comes from the pressure imbalance between front and rear caused by boundary layer growth and separation. Together they make profile drag.

cards.f: Give the flat-plate skin friction coefficients for laminar and turbulent boundary layers.
cards.b: Laminar (Blasius): Cf = 1.328/√Re. Turbulent (approximate): Cf = 0.074/Re^(1/5), with Re based on plate length.

cards.f: Why does a turbulent boundary layer resist separation better than a laminar one?
cards.b: Turbulent mixing brings high-momentum fluid close to the wall, so the near-wall flow can advance further against an adverse pressure gradient before it reverses.

cards.f: What causes an aerofoil to stall?
cards.b: At high angle of attack the adverse pressure gradient on the upper surface becomes so steep that the boundary layer separates. Lift falls sharply and drag and nose-down moment change abruptly.

cards.f: How do slotted flaps and leading-edge slats increase CLmax?
cards.b: Flaps increase effective camber, and often chord, raising lift at a given α. Slots and slats feed high-energy air over the upper surface, delaying separation to higher α.

cards.f: Define aspect ratio.
cards.b: AR = b²/S, which equals span divided by mean chord for a rectangular wing.

cards.f: What physically causes induced drag?
cards.b: Tip vortices and the trailing vortex sheet induce downwash at the wing. This tilts the local lift vector backwards, and the rearward component is induced drag.

cards.f: Give the induced drag coefficient for a general wing.
cards.b: CDi = CL²/(πeAR), where e is the span efficiency factor. e = 1 for elliptic lift distribution, which gives minimum induced drag.

cards.f: How does induced drag vary with speed in level flight?
cards.b: Di = W²/(½ρV²πb²e), so it is proportional to 1/V² and dominates at low speed.

cards.f: Give the finite-wing lift slope from lifting-line theory.
cards.b: a = a0/[1 + a0/(πAR)] for elliptic loading. Lower aspect ratio gives a shallower lift curve.

cards.f: What is the maximum lift-to-drag ratio for a parabolic drag polar?
cards.b: (L/D)max = 1/(2√(k·CD0)), reached at CL* = √(CD0/k), where induced drag equals zero-lift drag.

cards.f: Why is washout used on many wings?
cards.b: Twisting the tips to a lower incidence makes the root stall first. Aileron control is kept and wing drop is less likely, and the twist can also bring the lift distribution closer to elliptic.

cards.f: How do winglets reduce induced drag?
cards.b: They change the spanwise loading and the shape of the trailing vortex wake, raising effective span. The cost is added wetted area and higher wing-root bending moment.

cards.f: Why might a designer not simply choose a very high aspect ratio?
cards.b: A longer, more slender wing has a higher root bending moment and lower stiffness, so it needs more structure (weight), may have aeroelastic problems and has limited internal volume and airport gate width.

cards.f: Doubling the span at constant weight, speed and e changes induced drag by what factor?
cards.b: Di ∝ W²/(qb²), so doubling b reduces induced drag to one quarter.

cards.f: Give the isentropic stagnation temperature relation.
cards.b: T0/T = 1 + ½(γ − 1)M², which is 1 + 0.2M² for air.

cards.f: Below what Mach number can flow usually be treated as incompressible, and why?
cards.b: About M = 0.3, where density varies by less than about 5% from its stagnation value.

cards.f: State the Prandtl–Glauert rule.
cards.b: Cp = Cp0/√(1 − M∞²). It scales incompressible pressure coefficients for subsonic compressibility and is not valid near M = 1.

cards.f: Define critical Mach number.
cards.b: The free-stream Mach number at which the local flow somewhere on the body first reaches M = 1.

cards.f: How does wing sweep delay compressibility drag rise?
cards.b: Pressure distribution depends mainly on the velocity component normal to the leading edge, M·cos Λ. Sweep reduces this component, raising the free-stream Mach number for drag divergence.

cards.f: What happens across a normal shock wave?
cards.b: Flow goes from supersonic to subsonic. Static pressure, density and temperature rise, stagnation temperature stays constant, and stagnation pressure falls as entropy increases.

cards.f: Give M2, p2/p1 and p02/p01 for a normal shock at M1 = 2.
State the area–velocity relation and its meaning.
cards.b: dA/A = (M² − 1)dV/V. Subsonic flow accelerates in a converging duct, supersonic flow in a diverging duct, and M = 1 can occur only at a throat.

cards.f: What is the critical pressure ratio for choking in air?
cards.b: p*/p0 = (2/(γ + 1))^(γ/(γ−1)) = 0.528. When the back pressure falls below this, the throat chokes and mass flow cannot increase further.

cards.f: What is the Mach angle at M = 2?
cards.b: μ = arcsin(1/M) = arcsin(0.5) = 30°.

cards.f: Write the general thrust equation for a jet engine.
cards.b: F = ṁ(Ve − V0) + (pe − pa)Ae, neglecting fuel mass flow. The second term is pressure thrust.

cards.f: Define propulsive efficiency.
cards.b: ηp = thrust power/(rate of kinetic energy added to the air) = 2/(1 + Ve/V0). It approaches 1 as jet velocity approaches flight speed.

cards.f: Why do civil airliners use high-bypass turbofans?
cards.b: Accelerating a large mass of air by a small amount gives the required thrust with high propulsive efficiency, lower fuel burn and less jet noise.

cards.f: Give the ideal Brayton cycle thermal efficiency.
cards.b: ηth = 1 − 1/rp^((γ−1)/γ). For rp = 25 and γ = 1.4, ηth = 0.60.

cards.f: What is TSFC?
cards.b: Thrust-specific fuel consumption: fuel mass flow divided by thrust, e.g. kg/(N·h). It reflects overall efficiency at a given flight speed.

cards.f: Why are turboprops limited to lower cruise Mach numbers?
cards.b: Propeller tips move at the vector sum of rotational and forward speed, so they become transonic near cruise speeds of about M 0.6–0.7. Compressibility losses then cut propeller efficiency.

cards.f: State the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation.
cards.b: Δv = ve·ln(m0/mf), where ve = Isp·g0 is the effective exhaust velocity and m0/mf the mass ratio.

cards.f: How is overall efficiency related to thermal and propulsive efficiency?
cards.b: η0 = ηth × ηp. It is the thrust power divided by the rate of fuel energy release.

cards.f: What limits the thermal efficiency of a real gas turbine?
cards.b: Compressor and turbine losses, combustion pressure loss and, above all, the turbine entry temperature that blade materials and cooling can tolerate. Higher pressure ratio needs higher temperature to keep specific work up.

cards.f: Why is hydrogen hard to use in conventional airliner layouts?
cards.b: It has very high energy per kilogram but low energy per unit volume, even as a cryogenic liquid. It needs large insulated tanks that cannot easily fit in thin wings.

cards.f: Give the stall speed equation.
cards.b: Vs = √(2W/(ρSCLmax)). Stall speed rises with weight and altitude (in TAS) and falls with flap deflection.

cards.f: How does the stall speed change in a 60° banked level turn?
cards.b: n = 1/cos 60° = 2, so the stall speed rises by √2, about 41%.

cards.f: Give the turn radius and turn rate in a level turn.
cards.b: r = V²/(g·tan φ) and ω = g·tan φ/V. A tighter, faster turn needs more bank and a higher load factor.

cards.f: At what speed does a jet achieve maximum range?
cards.b: At 3^(1/4)·VMD ≈ 1.32 VMD, where CL = CL*/√3 and √CL/CD is a maximum.

cards.f: At what speeds does a propeller aircraft achieve maximum range and endurance?
cards.b: Maximum range at VMD (max L/D). Maximum endurance at the minimum power speed VMP ≈ 0.76 VMD.

cards.f: How is rate of climb related to excess power?
cards.b: ROC = (T − D)V/W = (power available − power required)/W.

cards.f: How far can a glider with L/D = 18 travel from 1000 m in still air?
cards.b: Distance = height × L/D = 1000 × 18 = 18 km. The glide angle is arctan(1/18) = 3.2°.

cards.f: State the Breguet range equation for a jet.
cards.b: R = (V/c)(L/D)·ln(W0/W1), with c the thrust-specific fuel consumption in consistent units (per second) and W0/W1 the initial-to-final weight ratio.

cards.f: What is the 'back of the drag curve'?
cards.b: The speed range below VMD, where flying slower needs more thrust. Speed is then unstable, because a speed loss increases drag and causes further slowing unless the pilot adds thrust.

cards.f: How does a hot day affect take-off distance?
cards.b: Higher density altitude lowers air density. Thrust or power falls, and the true lift-off speed for a given EAS rises, so the ground roll lengthens.

cards.f: What is the condition for longitudinal static stability?
cards.b: dCm/dα < 0 about the centre of gravity, so a nose-up disturbance produces a nose-down restoring moment.

cards.f: Define static margin.
cards.b: Kn = hn − h, the distance of the CG ahead of the neutral point as a fraction of mean aerodynamic chord. It must be positive for static stability.

cards.f: Define tail volume coefficient.
cards.b: V̄H = St·lt/(S·c̄), the tail area times its arm divided by wing area times mean chord. It measures the tail's stabilising power.

cards.f: What sets the forward CG limit?
cards.b: The elevator must have enough authority to trim and flare at low speed with flaps down, and stick forces must stay acceptable.

cards.f: What gives directional (weathercock) stability?
cards.b: Mainly the fin, which produces a restoring yawing moment in sideslip (Cnβ > 0). The fuselage forward of the CG is destabilising.

cards.f: What gives the dihedral effect (Clβ < 0)?
cards.b: Geometric dihedral, a high wing position and wing sweepback. Each makes the wing on the side of the sideslip lift more and roll the aircraft away.

cards.f: Describe the phugoid mode.
cards.b: A slow, lightly damped oscillation in which height and speed are exchanged at nearly constant angle of attack. Lanchester's approximation gives a period of π√2·V/g.

cards.f: Describe Dutch roll and its usual cure.
cards.b: A coupled oscillation of yaw and roll, worsened by strong dihedral effect and weak directional stability. Swept-wing jets use yaw dampers that move the rudder automatically.

cards.f: What is adverse yaw and how is it reduced?
cards.b: The down-going aileron raises lift and induced drag on the rising wing, yawing the nose away from the turn. Differential ailerons, Frise ailerons, spoilers or coordinated rudder reduce it.

cards.f: Why do some fighters have relaxed or negative static stability?
cards.b: It reduces trim drag and makes the aircraft more agile. Fly-by-wire flight control computers supply artificial stability that the pilot could not provide unaided.

cards.f: Define limit load and ultimate load.
cards.b: Limit load is the maximum load expected in service, carried without permanent deformation. Ultimate load is 1.5 × limit and must be carried without failure.

cards.f: What is the CS-25 positive limit manoeuvring load factor?
cards.b: n = 2.1 + 24 000/(W + 10 000) with W in lb, not less than 2.5 and not more than 3.8. Large transports therefore use 2.5.

cards.f: What does the stall boundary on a V–n diagram represent?
cards.b: The maximum load factor the wing can generate at each speed, n = (V/Vs)². It meets the positive limit load factor at the manoeuvre speed VA.

cards.f: Give the hoop and longitudinal stresses in a pressurised cylindrical fuselage.
cards.b: σh = pr/t and σl = pr/(2t), so hoop stress is twice longitudinal stress.

cards.f: State the Bredt–Batho shear flow result.
cards.b: For a single-cell closed thin-walled section in pure torsion, q = T/(2A), where A is the area enclosed by the wall mid-line. Shear stress is τ = q/t.

cards.f: What are the roles of spars, ribs and stringers in a wing?
cards.b: Spar caps carry bending and spar webs carry shear. Ribs keep the aerofoil shape, transfer loads and limit panel buckling length. Stringers stiffen the skin and share bending loads.

cards.f: Distinguish safe-life, fail-safe and damage-tolerant design.
cards.b: Safe-life parts are replaced before a set life. Fail-safe structures have alternative load paths if one member fails. Damage tolerance assumes cracks exist and sets inspections to catch them before they become critical.

cards.f: What did the Comet 1 accidents of 1954 reveal?
cards.b: Fatigue cracks grew from stress concentrations at corners of fuselage cut-outs under repeated pressurisation cycles. This led to full-scale fatigue testing and fail-safe thinking.

cards.f: Why is 2024 aluminium used on lower wing skins and 7075 on upper skins?
cards.b: Lower skins are in tension, so the fatigue and damage tolerance of 2024 matter most. Upper skins are in compression, where the higher strength of 7075 resists buckling and yield.

cards.f: Why does a higher wing loading reduce gust response?
cards.b: The gust load factor increment is Δn = ρ0·VE·a·U/(2W/S). A higher W/S gives a smaller Δn for the same gust, so heavily loaded aircraft ride more smoothly.

questions.q: What is the ISA sea-level temperature?
questions.why: ISA sea level is 15 °C, which is 288.15 K. 216.65 K is the temperature of the lower stratosphere.

questions.q: In the ISA, the speed of sound at 15 km altitude is closest to:
questions.why: Between 11 and 20 km the ISA temperature is constant at 216.65 K, so a = √(1.4 × 287 × 216.65) ≈ 295 m/s.

questions.q: Explain the difference between indicated, calibrated, equivalent and true airspeed, and state which matters for structural loads and which for navigation.
markScheme: IAS: read directly from the airspeed indicator (pitot-static pressure difference)
CAS: IAS corrected for instrument and position (static source) errors
EAS: CAS corrected for compressibility; gives true dynamic pressure ½ρ0VE²; TAS = EAS/√σ
Loads, stall and handling depend on EAS (dynamic pressure); navigation, Mach number and ground speed calculations use TAS
questions.modelAnswer: Indicated airspeed is what the airspeed indicator shows from the pitot-static pressure difference. Calibrated airspeed corrects IAS for instrument error and for position error in the static source. Equivalent airspeed further corrects CAS for compressibility, so that ½ρ0VE² equals the true dynamic pressure. True airspeed is the actual speed relative to the air, V = VE/√σ, and exceeds EAS at altitude. Aerodynamic loads, stalling speeds and handling depend on dynamic pressure, so they are specified in EAS. Navigation, flight time and Mach number use TAS.

questions.q: Captain Lena Okafor is cruising at a pressure altitude of 8000 m at a true airspeed of 220 m/s. (a) Assuming ISA conditions, calculate the temperature, pressure, density, speed of sound, Mach number, equivalent airspeed and dynamic pressure. (b) The next day the aircraft flies at the same pressure altitude and true airspeed, but the air is 15 K warmer than ISA (ISA+15). Recalculate the density, Mach number and EAS. (c) Estimate the density altitude on the warm day. (d) Explain the operational consequences of the warm day for cruise and for take-off from a high, hot airfield.
markScheme: ISA+15: same pressure 35.6 kPa, T = 251.15 K, ρ = 0.494 kg/m³
Density altitude ≈ 8500 m (ISA altitude where ρ = 0.494 kg/m³)
Cruise: lower density means lower EAS/dynamic pressure for the same TAS, so higher CL and possibly a lower optimum altitude; lower Mach number for the same TAS
Take-off: high density altitude reduces engine thrust and needs higher TAS for the same EAS lift-off speed, so longer runs, reduced climb gradient and possibly payload restrictions
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) T = 288.15 − 0.0065 × 8000 = 236.15 K. p = 101 325 × (236.15/288.15)^5.256 = 35.6 kPa. ρ = 35 600/(287.05 × 236.15) = 0.525 kg/m³, so σ = 0.429. a = √(1.4 × 287.05 × 236.15) = 308.1 m/s, giving M = 220/308.1 = 0.714. EAS = 220 × √0.429 = 144 m/s, and q = ½ × 0.525 × 220² = 12.7 kPa.

(b) Pressure altitude fixes pressure, so p is still 35.6 kPa, but T = 251.15 K. Then ρ = 35 600/(287.05 × 251.15) = 0.494 kg/m³ and σ = 0.403. The speed of sound rises to √(1.4 × 287.05 × 251.15) = 317.7 m/s, so M = 0.692. EAS = 220 × √0.403 = 139.7 m/s.

(c) The density altitude is the ISA height with ρ = 0.494 kg/m³. Solving (T/288.15)^4.256 = 0.403 gives T = 232.7 K, so h ≈ 8500 m, about 500 m above the pressure altitude.

(d) In cruise, the same true airspeed now gives less dynamic pressure. To support the weight, the aircraft must fly at a higher CL or a higher TAS, which may move the optimum altitude down. Because the speed of sound is higher, the Mach number is lower for a given TAS. Engine thrust at altitude also falls in warm air. At a high, hot airfield the same effects are larger. The wings need a higher true airspeed for the same EAS at lift-off, and the engines deliver less thrust because the air is less dense. Take-off runs lengthen and climb gradients fall. Operators may have to cut payload or fuel, or schedule departures for cooler times of day.

questions.q: According to thin aerofoil theory, about which point is the pitching moment coefficient independent of angle of attack?
questions.why: The aerodynamic centre of a thin aerofoil is at c/4. The centre of pressure moves with α for a cambered section.

questions.q: A flat plate of length 2 m sits in an airflow at 60 m/s (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³, ν = 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s). Calculate the Reynolds number and compare the skin friction drag per metre width (both sides) for a fully laminar and a fully turbulent boundary layer.
markScheme: Laminar Cf = 1.328/√Re = 4.70 × 10⁻⁴; turbulent Cf = 0.074/Re^0.2 = 3.08 × 10⁻³
Laminar ≈ 4.1 N/m, turbulent ≈ 27.2 N/m: turbulent about 6.6 times higher
questions.modelAnswer: Re = VL/ν = 60 × 2/1.5 × 10⁻⁵ = 8.0 × 10⁶. For a laminar layer, Cf = 1.328/√(8 × 10⁶) = 4.70 × 10⁻⁴. For a turbulent layer, Cf ≈ 0.074/(8 × 10⁶)^0.2 = 3.08 × 10⁻³. The dynamic pressure is q = ½ × 1.225 × 60² = 2205 Pa. Drag per metre width on both sides is D = 2CfqL, which gives 4.1 N/m for the laminar case and 27.2 N/m for the turbulent case. The turbulent layer gives about 6.6 times the skin friction. Laminar flow is unlikely to last over the whole plate at this Reynolds number, but the comparison explains why natural laminar flow surfaces are attractive.

questions.q: Students at Wexley University test a 1.5 m chord wing section, spanning the tunnel, at 50 m/s in sea-level air (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³, μ = 1.789 × 10⁻⁵ Pa·s). (a) Calculate the Reynolds number. (b) For a symmetric section at α = 6°, use thin aerofoil theory to estimate the lift coefficient and the lift per metre span. (c) State the pitching moment coefficient about the quarter chord and about the leading edge, and the position of the centre of pressure. (d) A cambered section with αL0 = −2° is tested at the same α. Repeat (b) and explain how its pitching moment behaviour differs. (e) Explain why measured lift will fall below these predictions at high α.
markScheme: Symmetric: cm,c/4 = 0; cm,LE = −cl/4 = −0.164; centre of pressure at quarter chord
Cambered section has negative (nose-down) cm,ac constant with α; centre of pressure lies aft of c/4 and moves forward towards c/4 as cl increases
Real lift slope slightly below 2π due to viscous effects (boundary layer displacement)
At high α the adverse pressure gradient causes boundary layer separation, so lift curve flattens and stalls at clmax (around 1.2–1.6)
Tunnel corrections (blockage, wall interference) may also be needed
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Re = 1.225 × 50 × 1.5/1.789 × 10⁻⁵ = 5.1 × 10⁶.

(b) α = 6° = 0.1047 rad, so cl = 2π × 0.1047 = 0.658. The dynamic pressure is q = ½ × 1.225 × 50² = 1531 Pa, so the lift per metre span is L' = 1531 × 1.5 × 0.658 = 1.51 kN/m.

(c) A symmetric thin aerofoil has its aerodynamic centre and centre of pressure both at the quarter chord, so cm,c/4 = 0. About the leading edge, with nose-up positive, cm,LE = −cl/4 = −0.164.

(d) With αL0 = −2°, the effective incidence is 8° = 0.1396 rad, so cl = 2π × 0.1396 = 0.877 and L' = 1531 × 1.5 × 0.877 = 2.02 kN/m. Camber shifts the lift curve to the left without changing its slope. It also produces a negative, nose-down moment about the aerodynamic centre that stays constant with α. The centre of pressure therefore lies behind the quarter chord and moves forward towards it as lift increases. This is why the aerodynamic centre, not the centre of pressure, is used in stability analysis.

(e) Thin aerofoil theory is inviscid. In reality, the boundary layer displaces the effective shape and the lift slope is slightly lower, about 0.1 per degree. As α increases, the suction peak and the adverse pressure gradient over the upper surface grow until the boundary layer separates, usually spreading forward from the trailing edge. The lift curve then bends over and the section stalls at clmax, typically 1.2–1.6, with a rise in drag and a change in moment. Wind tunnel results also need corrections for blockage and wall interference before they can be compared with theory.

questions.q: Evaluate the proposition that 'a turbulent boundary layer is always undesirable on an aircraft'. Your answer should explain how boundary layers develop over a wing, quantify the skin friction penalty of turbulence using flat-plate relations for Re = 8 × 10⁶, and discuss separation, stall, high-lift devices and practical drag reduction measures, using examples from both cruise and low-speed flight.
markScheme: Boundary layer concept (Prandtl, 1904): viscous effects confined to a thin layer; laminar near the leading edge, transition, turbulent downstream
Transition depends on Reynolds number, pressure gradient, surface roughness, and disturbances; favourable gradients delay it
Quantification: laminar Cf = 1.328/√Re = 4.7 × 10⁻⁴; turbulent Cf ≈ 0.074/Re^0.2 = 3.1 × 10⁻³ at Re = 8 × 10⁶, about 6–7 times more skin friction
Supports proposition: turbulent skin friction dominates cruise profile drag of airliners; natural or hybrid laminar flow wings aim to keep laminar flow
Counter: turbulent layers carry more momentum near the wall and resist separation in adverse pressure gradients
Separation drives pressure drag and stall; laminar separation bubbles at low Re can cause early stall or drag
Vortex generators deliberately trip/mix the boundary layer to delay separation (e.g. ahead of control surfaces)
High-lift devices: slots/slats energise the upper surface boundary layer; flaps rely on attached flow
Bluff bodies: earlier transition can reduce total drag (drag crisis of spheres)
Conclusion: undesirable for skin friction in cruise but beneficial where separation control matters; designers manage where transition occurs
questions.modelAnswer:
The proposition is only half right. Prandtl's boundary layer concept (1904) confines viscous effects to a thin layer next to the surface. On a wing, this layer starts laminar at the leading edge, then transitions to turbulence at a point set by Reynolds number, pressure gradient, surface roughness, contamination and free-stream disturbances. A favourable pressure gradient, with pressure falling along the surface, delays transition. An adverse gradient promotes it.

The skin friction penalty is large. At Re = 8 × 10⁶, a laminar flat plate has Cf = 1.328/√Re = 4.7 × 10⁻⁴, while a turbulent one has Cf ≈ 0.074/Re^0.2 = 3.1 × 10⁻³, roughly 6–7 times greater. Turbulent skin friction makes up most of an airliner's profile drag in cruise. That is why natural and hybrid laminar flow wings, smooth surfaces and careful pressure-distribution design receive so much attention. In this sense turbulence is undesirable.

Yet turbulence brings high-momentum fluid close to the wall, so a turbulent layer can travel much further against an adverse pressure gradient before separating. Separation is far more damaging than extra friction. It causes large pressure drag, loss of lift, buffet and stall. At low Reynolds numbers, laminar layers may separate and form separation bubbles that degrade performance. Engineers therefore often promote turbulence on purpose. Vortex generators ahead of ailerons or on engine nacelles mix energetic air into the boundary layer and delay separation. Slots and slats re-energise the upper-surface flow so the wing reaches a higher CLmax. On bluff bodies, early transition delays separation and can cut total drag sharply, as in the drag crisis of a sphere.

In conclusion, turbulent boundary layers are costly where friction dominates, over smooth, attached cruise surfaces. They are valuable wherever separation threatens. Good design controls where and when transition occurs rather than trying to remove turbulence altogether.

questions.q: A wing of aspect ratio 8 and span efficiency 0.85 flies at CL = 0.5. Its induced drag coefficient is closest to:
Using Di = W²/(½ρV²πb²e), explain why induced drag matters most during take-off, climb and approach, and why span is a more fundamental parameter than aspect ratio.
markScheme: Di ∝ 1/V², so induced drag is largest at low speeds (take-off, climb, approach) where high CL is needed
Di ∝ W², so heavy aircraft at take-off are most affected
Di depends on span loading W/b; at fixed weight and speed, increasing span reduces Di as 1/b², regardless of chord
Aspect ratio matters only via b² = AR·S; a high AR with small area does not help if b is small; gate/structural limits on span
questions.modelAnswer: Writing induced drag in dimensional form shows that it is proportional to W²/(V²b²). At low speed, the wing must work at a high CL to support the weight, so induced drag rises as 1/V² and dominates during take-off, the initial climb and the approach, when the aircraft is also at its heaviest. In cruise at high speed, zero-lift drag matters more. The formula contains span directly, not aspect ratio. For a given weight and speed, induced drag depends on the span loading W/b, and doubling the span cuts it by a factor of four. Aspect ratio matters only because b² = AR·S. Raising AR by shrinking chord at fixed span brings no induced-drag benefit.

questions.q: Velo Aerospace is comparing two wing designs for a 50 kN utility aircraft with a wing area of 30 m², flying at 50 m/s at sea level. Design A has an aspect ratio of 6 and design B an aspect ratio of 10. Both have e = 0.85 and a zero-lift drag coefficient of 0.025. (a) Calculate the lift coefficient and the span of each wing. (b) Calculate the induced drag coefficient and induced drag of each. (c) Calculate the maximum lift-to-drag ratio and the corresponding CL for each. (d) Using lifting-line theory with a0 = 2π/rad and elliptic loading, compare the wing lift-curve slopes. (e) Discuss the wider design trade-offs of choosing design B.
markScheme: CDi,B = 0.0444; Di,B = 2.04 kN (40% lower)
(L/D)max,B = 16.3 at CL = 0.82
B: better climb, glide, range and low-speed performance; steeper lift slope means larger gust response
B: higher root bending moment and lower stiffness so heavier structure, aeroelastic concerns, thinner chord reduces Reynolds number and fuel volume; hangar/span limits
Conclusion: justified for missions dominated by low-speed or long-endurance flight, subject to weight study
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) q = ½ × 1.225 × 50² = 1531 Pa and CL = 50 000/(1531 × 30) = 1.09. The spans are bA = √(6 × 30) = 13.4 m and bB = √(10 × 30) = 17.3 m.

(b) CDi,A = 1.09²/(π × 0.85 × 6) = 0.0739, giving Di,A = 0.0739 × 1531 × 30 = 3.40 kN. CDi,B = 1.09²/(π × 0.85 × 10) = 0.0444, giving Di,B = 2.04 kN. Design B cuts induced drag by 40% because its span is greater.

(c) kA = 1/(π × 0.85 × 6) = 0.0624 and kB = 0.0374. (L/D)max,A = 1/(2√(0.0624 × 0.025)) = 12.7 at CL* = √(0.025/0.0624) = 0.63. (L/D)max,B = 16.3 at CL* = 0.82.

(d) aA = 2π/(1 + 2π/(6π)) = 2π/1.333 = 4.71/rad and aB = 2π/1.2 = 5.24/rad. B reaches a given CL at a lower angle of attack.

(e) Design B gives better glide ratio, climb rate, range and endurance, and lower power needed at low speed. That matters for a utility aircraft that often operates slowly. Its steeper lift slope, however, makes it respond more to gusts, which affects ride comfort and gust loads. Structurally, a longer and narrower wing has a greater root bending moment and less depth for the spar, so it needs more material and may be heavier and more flexible. That raises aeroelastic and flutter concerns and offsets part of the aerodynamic gain. Smaller chords reduce internal fuel volume and Reynolds number, and the larger span can cause hangar, taxiway or transport problems. The choice should rest on a mission analysis that includes wing weight. B is likely to win where low-speed and endurance segments dominate.

questions.q: An airliner operated by Northlight Air has mass 60 000 kg, wing area 122 m², aspect ratio 9.5, Oswald factor 0.80 and CD0 = 0.020. It cruises at M 0.78 at 11 000 m in ISA (T = 216.65 K, ρ = 0.364 kg/m³, a = 295.1 m/s). (a) Calculate the true airspeed, lift coefficient, drag coefficient, lift-to-drag ratio, drag and the share of drag due to lift. (b) Find (L/D)max, the CL at which it occurs and the minimum drag speed at this altitude. (c) Theory says jets achieve maximum range at about 1.32 VMD. Calculate this speed and its Mach number, and explain why the airline does not fly at it. (d) Critically assess two design changes that could improve cruise L/D.
markScheme: L/D = 0.50/0.0305 = 16.4; D = W/(L/D) = 35.9 kN; lift-dependent share ≈ 34%

Such Mach number exceeds drag-divergence Mach for this wing, so wave drag would destroy the assumed parabolic polar (CD0 constant); actual cruise Mach chosen near drag divergence, balancing fuel and time costs
Higher aspect ratio / span (folding tips, strut-bracing) reduces k; trade weight and gate limits
Laminar flow, riblets, reduced wetted area reduce CD0; or winglets; or supercritical aerofoils allowing higher Mach at same drag
Notes that the optimum also depends on weight falling during cruise (cruise-climb/step climbs)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) V = 0.78 × 295.1 = 230 m/s and q = ½ × 0.364 × 230² = 9.64 kPa. W = 60 000 × 9.81 = 588.6 kN, so CL = 588 600/(9640 × 122) = 0.50. k = 1/(π × 0.80 × 9.5) = 0.0419, so CDi = 0.0419 × 0.50² = 0.0105 and CD = 0.0305. L/D = 0.50/0.0305 = 16.4, and drag = W/(L/D) = 35.9 kN. Lift-dependent drag is 0.0105/0.0305 ≈ 34% of the total.

(b) (L/D)max = 1/(2√(0.0419 × 0.020)) = 17.3 at CL* = √(0.020/0.0419) = 0.69. Then VMD = √(2 × 588 600/(0.364 × 122 × 0.69)) = 196 m/s, which is M 0.66.

(c) 1.316 × 196 = 258 m/s, which is M 0.87. The result assumes a parabolic polar with constant CD0. Near M 0.8 and above, shocks form on the wing and wave drag rises steeply beyond the drag-divergence Mach number. At M 0.87 this wing's drag would be far higher than the polar predicts, so the theoretical optimum is not real. Airlines cruise close to, but below, drag divergence. Many fly a little faster than the speed for maximum fuel range, because time-related costs (crew, maintenance, aircraft use) favour speed: the long-range cruise and cost-index concepts. Cruise-climbs or step climbs keep CL near its best value as fuel burns off.

(d) Increasing the span reduces k and is the most powerful lever on lift-dependent drag. But it adds wing weight and root bending moment, and airport gate limits may need folding wingtips, as on the Boeing 777X. Strut-bracing allows very high aspect ratio but adds interference drag and limits cruise Mach. Reducing CD0 through natural or hybrid laminar flow, riblets or less wetted area raises L/D directly. Laminar flow, however, is fragile to contamination and sweep, and supercritical sections that permit higher Mach must be balanced against thickness and structural weight. Winglets give a smaller, retrofittable gain.

questions.q: Across a stationary normal shock wave in a perfect gas, which quantity stays constant?
questions.why: The shock is adiabatic, so stagnation temperature is conserved. Entropy rises, so stagnation pressure falls.

questions.q: An aircraft flies at M 0.8 at 11 km (p = 22.63 kPa, T = 216.65 K). Calculate the stagnation pressure using the isentropic relation and compare it with the value given by incompressible Bernoulli. Comment on the result.
markScheme: Bernoulli: p0 = p + ½ρV² = 22.63 + 10.14 = 32.8 kPa
Bernoulli underestimates the pitot pressure rise by about 15%, so compressibility must be included above M ≈ 0.3 (basis of the CAS-to-EAS correction)
questions.modelAnswer: Isentropically, p0/p = (1 + 0.2 × 0.8²)^3.5 = 1.128^3.5 = 1.524, so p0 = 34.5 kPa and the pitot rise is 11.9 kPa. The density is ρ = 22 630/(287.05 × 216.65) = 0.364 kg/m³ and the speed is V = 0.8 × 295.1 = 236 m/s, so ½ρV² = 10.1 kPa and Bernoulli predicts p0 = 32.8 kPa. The incompressible formula underestimates the pressure rise by about 15%. Air compresses as it slows towards the stagnation point, so the pressure rise exceeds ½ρV². Above about M 0.3, airspeed systems must use the compressible relation, which is the source of the CAS-to-EAS correction.

questions.q: A supersonic research aircraft built by Altair Dynamics flies at M 2.0 at 11 km (p1 = 22.63 kPa, T1 = 216.65 K, γ = 1.4, R = 287 J/(kg·K)). A pitot probe on the nose has a normal shock standing just ahead of it. (a) Calculate the flight speed and free-stream stagnation temperature and pressure. (b) Using normal shock relations, find M2, p2, T2 and the flow speed just behind the shock, and verify continuity. (c) Find the stagnation pressure measured by the probe and the loss of stagnation pressure. (d) Show what Mach number would be wrongly deduced if the reading were treated with the subsonic isentropic relation, and explain how the probe should be interpreted.
markScheme: Stagnation pressure loss ≈ 49 kPa (28%), entropy rise
Subsonic formula: (1 + 0.2M²)^3.5 = 5.64 gives M ≈ 1.79, an underestimate
Use the Rayleigh pitot formula relating p02/p1 to M1, with a separate static pressure measurement; T0 is unchanged across the shock so total temperature probes still work
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) a1 = √(1.4 × 287 × 216.65) = 295.1 m/s, so V1 = 590 m/s. T01 = 216.65 × (1 + 0.2 × 4) = 390 K and p01 = 22.63 × 1.8^3.5 = 177 kPa.

(b) M2 = √[(1 + 0.2 × 4)/(1.4 × 4 − 0.2)] = √(1.8/5.4) = 0.577. p2/p1 = 1 + (2 × 1.4/2.4)(4 − 1) = 4.5, so p2 = 101.8 kPa. ρ2/ρ1 = 2.4 × 4/(2 + 0.4 × 4) = 2.67, so T2/T1 = 4.5/2.67 = 1.6875 and T2 = 365.6 K. a2 = √(1.4 × 287 × 365.6) = 383.3 m/s, so V2 = 0.577 × 383.3 = 221 m/s. Continuity requires ρ1V1 = ρ2V2, and V1/V2 = 590/221 = 2.67, which matches the density ratio. As a check on T0: T2(1 + 0.2 × 0.333) = 365.6 × 1.0667 = 390 K, unchanged as expected.

(c) p02/p01 = 0.721, so the probe senses p02 = 0.721 × 177 = 127.6 kPa, which is 5.64p1. About 49 kPa, or 28% of the free-stream stagnation pressure, is lost to the entropy rise in the shock.

(d) Treating 127.6/22.63 = 5.64 as an isentropic ratio, (1 + 0.2M²)^3.5 = 5.64 gives M = 1.79, about 10% too low. In supersonic flight the probe must be interpreted with the Rayleigh pitot formula, which combines the normal shock and the subsonic isentropic compression behind it. The free-stream static pressure must be measured separately, at a well-placed static port, to form p02/p1. Stagnation temperature is conserved across the shock, so total temperature probes can still give the static temperature once M is known.

questions.q: Orbis Propulsion is testing a convergent–divergent nozzle supplied with air at stagnation conditions p0 = 500 kPa and T0 = 500 K (γ = 1.4, R = 287 J/(kg·K)). The throat area is 0.010 m² and the nozzle is designed for an exit Mach number of 2.0. (a) Calculate the exit area, exit static pressure, temperature and velocity at design conditions. (b) Calculate the mass flow rate. (c) Calculate the thrust when the nozzle exhausts to a back pressure equal to the design exit pressure, and when it exhausts at sea level (pa = 101.3 kPa), assuming shock-free flow inside the nozzle. (d) Explain the flow regimes as back pressure varies, and the implications for rocket and engine nozzle design.
markScheme: ṁ = 0.0404 A*p0/√T0 (or full formula) = 9.04 kg/s; check via ρeVeAe
Matched thrust F = ṁVe = 6.04 kN
Sea level: F = ṁVe + (pe − pa)Ae = 6039 − 632 = 5.41 kN, over-expanded

Explains: high back pressure gives subsonic venturi flow; at critical value throat chokes; further reduction gives normal shock inside diverging section moving to exit; then over-expanded with oblique shocks outside; design condition; under-expanded with expansion fans
Mass flow fixed once choked, independent of back pressure

Implications: fixed rocket nozzles are a compromise across altitude (sea-level over-expansion, vacuum under-expansion); flow separation risk; variable nozzles in afterburning engines; altitude-compensating concepts
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) A/A* = (1/2)[(2/2.4)(1 + 0.2 × 4)]³ = 0.5 × 1.5³ = 1.6875, so Ae = 0.0169 m². T0/Te = 1.8, so Te = 277.8 K. p0/pe = 1.8^3.5 = 7.82, so pe = 63.9 kPa. ae = √(1.4 × 287 × 277.8) = 334 m/s, so Ve = 2 × 334 = 668 m/s.

(b) The choked mass flow is ṁ = A*·p0·√(γ/(RT0))·(2/(γ + 1))^((γ+1)/(2(γ−1))). For air this reduces to ṁ = 0.0404A*p0/√T0 = 0.0404 × 0.010 × 500 000/√500 = 9.04 kg/s. As a check, ρe = 63 900/(287 × 277.8) = 0.801 kg/m³, and ρeVeAe = 0.801 × 668 × 0.0169 = 9.04 kg/s.

(c) At design back pressure, F = ṁVe = 9.04 × 668 = 6.04 kN. At sea level, the pressure term is negative: F = 6039 + (63 900 − 101 300) × 0.0169 = 6039 − 632 = 5.41 kN. The nozzle is over-expanded and loses about 10% of its thrust.

(d) With back pressure only slightly below p0, the whole flow is subsonic and the nozzle acts as a venturi. Lowering the back pressure further brings the throat to M = 1. From then on the mass flow is fixed at 9.04 kg/s, whatever happens downstream. Lower still, the diverging section goes supersonic but ends in a normal shock, which moves towards the exit as back pressure falls. Below that, the internal flow is fully supersonic. If pa > pe the jet is over-expanded and oblique shocks form at the lip. At pa = pe the nozzle is at design. If pa < pe, expansion fans form outside and the jet is under-expanded, wasting potential thrust. A fixed-geometry rocket nozzle must compromise. Large area ratios suit vacuum, but at sea level they over-expand and risk flow separation and side loads. Launch-vehicle first stages therefore use moderate area ratios, and upper stages large ones. Afterburning jet engines use variable-area nozzles, and altitude-compensating concepts such as aerospikes aim to match pe to pa across the trajectory.

questions.q: An engine's jet velocity is twice its flight speed. Its propulsive efficiency is:

Calculate the ideal Brayton cycle thermal efficiency for an overall pressure ratio of 25 (γ = 1.4), and the compressor delivery temperature if the inlet is at 288 K. Explain why designers cannot simply keep increasing the pressure ratio.
markScheme: Higher rp raises compressor delivery temperature, reducing the temperature rise available in the combustor for a fixed turbine entry temperature, so specific work falls
Also limits from compressor stage count, small blade heights in the core, component losses and material limits; turbine entry temperature must rise in step
questions.modelAnswer: The ideal Brayton efficiency is ηth = 1 − rp^(−(γ−1)/γ) = 1 − 25^(−0.2857) = 1 − 0.399 = 0.60. The isentropic compressor delivery temperature is T2 = 288 × 25^0.2857 = 722 K. Raising the pressure ratio improves ideal efficiency but also raises T2. For a fixed turbine entry temperature, less heat can be added in the combustor, so the specific work falls and the engine must grow for the same thrust. High pressure ratios also mean many compressor stages, tiny rear blades with relatively larger losses, and hot compressor discs. So pressure ratio rises only alongside gains in materials and turbine cooling.

questions.q: Two engine concepts are proposed for a regional jet cruising at 200 m/s, each required to produce 20 kN of thrust. Concept A (a low-bypass design from Tamsin Engines) accelerates 50 kg/s of air. Concept B (a high-bypass design from Rook Propulsion) accelerates 200 kg/s. Assume fully expanded jets and ignore fuel mass. (a) Calculate the jet velocity of each concept. (b) Calculate the propulsive efficiency of each. (c) Calculate the thrust power and the rate of kinetic energy wasted in each wake, and confirm your efficiencies. (d) If both cores have a thermal efficiency of 0.45, find the overall efficiencies and the ratio of fuel flows. (e) Discuss the practical penalties of concept B.
markScheme: B: Ve − V0 = 100 m/s, so Ve = 300 m/s
Thrust power = FV0 = 4.0 MW for both
Wasted KE rate = ½ṁ(Ve − V0)²: A 4.0 MW, B 1.0 MW
Fuel flow ∝ 1/η0, so A burns 1.6 times the fuel of B

Penalties of B: larger fan and nacelle diameter (drag, weight), ground clearance, installation effects; thrust lapse with speed; need for a gearbox or low-pressure turbine with many stages; noise benefit noted
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) For a fully expanded jet, F = ṁ(Ve − V0). For A, Ve − V0 = 20 000/50 = 400 m/s, so Ve = 600 m/s. For B, Ve − V0 = 100 m/s, so Ve = 300 m/s.

(b) ηp,A = 2/(1 + 600/200) = 0.50 and ηp,B = 2/(1 + 300/200) = 0.80.

(c) Both produce thrust power FV0 = 20 000 × 200 = 4.0 MW. The kinetic energy left in the wake each second is ½ṁ(Ve − V0)². For A that is ½ × 50 × 400² = 4.0 MW, and for B ½ × 200 × 100² = 1.0 MW. Hence ηp,A = 4/(4 + 4) = 0.50 and ηp,B = 4/(4 + 1) = 0.80, which confirms (b).

(d) η0 = ηth × ηp, giving 0.225 for A and 0.36 for B. For the same thrust power, fuel flow is inversely proportional to overall efficiency, so A burns 0.36/0.225 = 1.6 times as much fuel as B.

(e) B achieves its efficiency by moving four times the air, which needs a much larger fan. The nacelle grows in diameter, adding weight and wetted-area drag that eat into the gain. Mounting the engine under a low wing becomes hard because of ground clearance, and it may need a longer landing gear or a different wing. The fan should turn slowly to keep tip speeds subsonic, which calls for a reduction gearbox or a many-stage low-pressure turbine, adding weight and complexity. High-bypass engines also lose thrust faster as flight speed rises, which suits subsonic airliners but not fast aircraft. B is quieter because its jet velocity is lower. For a regional jet, the fuel saving would normally outweigh these penalties.

questions.q: 'Future reductions in aviation fuel burn will come mainly from ever-higher bypass ratios.' Critically discuss this claim. Your answer should use the relationship between overall, thermal and propulsive efficiency, include at least one quantitative illustration, and consider alternative routes such as core thermal efficiency, airframe improvements, open rotors and alternative fuels, as well as the limits each faces.
markScheme: Defines η0 = ηth × ηp and links fuel burn to η0 and to L/D and weight via the Breguet range equation
Explains ηp = 2/(1 + Ve/V0): higher bypass lowers Ve and raises ηp; diminishing returns as ηp approaches 1
Quantitative illustration (e.g. Ve/V0 = 3 gives 0.50; 1.5 gives 0.80; or Brayton rp 25 gives 0.60, rp 40 gives 0.65)
Penalties of very high bypass: fan diameter, nacelle drag and weight, installation, ground clearance, gearbox; so net installed benefit shrinks
Core thermal efficiency: higher pressure ratio and turbine entry temperature, materials and cooling, smaller cores, intercooling/recuperation concepts
Open rotors/unducted fans remove nacelle constraints and reach very high effective bypass, but noise, certification, blade-off and cruise Mach limits
Airframe: higher span/laminar flow/lighter composite structures improve L/D and weight, equally important in Breguet
Operations: air traffic management, load factors, continuous descent
Alternative fuels: SAF reduces lifecycle CO₂ without changing fuel burn; hydrogen and electrification change the problem; non-CO₂ effects (contrails)
Balanced conclusion: bypass ratio is one lever with diminishing returns; gains will come from a combination
questions.modelAnswer:
Fuel burn for a given mission depends on the overall efficiency η0 = ηth × ηp, and through the Breguet range equation also on lift-to-drag ratio and structural weight. Bypass ratio acts mainly on propulsive efficiency, ηp = 2/(1 + Ve/V0). Raising bypass lowers jet velocity. Moving from Ve/V0 = 3 to 1.5 lifts ηp from 0.50 to 0.80, a 60% gain, and the jump from turbojets to high-bypass turbofans was one of the great efficiency advances in aviation. The function saturates, however. Going from Ve/V0 = 1.5 to 1.2 gives only 0.91, and every step needs a much larger fan.

Larger fans bring heavier, draggier nacelles, installation interference, ground clearance limits under low wings, and the need for gearboxes to keep fan tips subsonic. Beyond a point, the installed gain is cancelled. Open rotors remove the nacelle and reach very high effective bypass ratios, but they face noise, blade-containment and certification challenges and lower cruise Mach numbers.

Core thermal efficiency is the other half of η0. Ideal Brayton efficiency rises from 0.60 at a pressure ratio of 25 to 0.65 at 40. Real gains depend on turbine materials, ceramic matrix composites, cooling and smaller, highly loaded cores. Airframe advances matter equally in the Breguet equation. Higher-span wings (with folding tips), laminar flow and lighter composite structures can deliver gains comparable to engine improvements. Operational measures such as better air traffic management and continuous descents also contribute.

Fuel burn is not the same as climate impact. Sustainable aviation fuels cut lifecycle CO₂ with little change to fuel burn, while hydrogen changes the design problem through tank volume and creates different non-CO₂ effects such as contrails. Electrification suits only short, small aircraft with today's batteries.

The claim therefore overstates one lever. Higher bypass has delivered and will keep delivering gains, but with diminishing returns. Future reductions will come from engine core, propulsor, airframe, operations and fuel together.

questions.q: An aircraft in a steady level turn at 60° bank experiences a load factor of:

A light aircraft of mass 1100 kg has wing area 16.2 m² and CLmax = 1.5. Find its sea-level stall speed in straight flight and in a 45° banked level turn, and the radius and rate of a 45° turn at 45 m/s.
markScheme: ω = g tan φ/V = 0.218 rad/s = 12.5°/s
questions.modelAnswer: W = 1100 × 9.81 = 10 791 N, so Vs = √(2 × 10 791/(1.225 × 16.2 × 1.5)) = 26.9 m/s. In a 45° bank, n = 1/cos 45° = 1.414, and the stall speed rises with √n to 26.9 × 1.189 = 32.0 m/s. At 45 m/s, tan 45° = 1, so the turn radius is r = 45²/(9.81 × 1) = 206 m and the turn rate is ω = 9.81/45 = 0.218 rad/s, about 12.5° per second. The margin above the turning stall speed is about 40%, but steeper banks erode it quickly.

questions.q: A glider with a best L/D of 18 is at 10 000 m. Estimate its still-air glide distance and glide angle, and explain how a headwind would change the best speed to fly.
markScheme: Distance = h × L/D = 10 × 18 = 180 km
Glide angle = arctan(1/18) = 3.2°
Into a headwind the pilot should fly faster than best-L/D speed to maximise distance over the ground (and slower in a tailwind)
questions.modelAnswer: In still air the glide path angle satisfies tan γ = D/L = 1/18, so γ = 3.2°, and the distance covered is h × L/D = 10 km × 18 = 180 km, ignoring the change in density with height. Flying at best L/D maximises distance through the air. Into a headwind, distance over the ground matters, and time spent at low speed lets the wind carry the glider back. The pilot should therefore fly faster than the best-L/D speed, accepting a steeper glide through the air to improve the ground glide ratio. In a tailwind, slightly slower is better.

questions.q: Kestrel Airways operates a twin-jet with take-off mass 70 000 kg. Each engine produces 60 kN in the climb. (a) In the initial climb at 150 m/s TAS, the aircraft has L/D = 16. Calculate the drag, the climb angle and the rate of climb. (b) In cruise at 230 m/s with L/D = 17 and TSFC = 0.60 per hour, calculate the still-air range if 25% of the initial cruise weight is fuel burned. (c) Calculate the endurance for the same fuel. (d) Find the fuel fraction needed for a 5000 km stage. (e) Evaluate the separate effects on range of a 10% improvement in L/D and a 10% reduction in zero-fuel weight, and comment on the assumptions of the Breguet equation.
markScheme: 10% better L/D raises range by 10% (linear)
10% lighter zero-fuel weight raises W0/W1 for the same fuel load, increasing range through the log term (or allows more payload/fuel)
Assumptions: constant V, L/D and c (cruise-climb), no climb/descent/reserves, still air
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) W = 70 000 × 9.81 = 686.7 kN, so D = 686.7/16 = 42.9 kN. Total thrust is 120 kN, so sin γ = (120 − 42.9)/686.7 = 0.112, giving γ = 6.4°. The rate of climb is 150 × 0.112 = 16.8 m/s, about 3300 ft/min.

(b) Converting TSFC, c = 0.60/3600 = 1.667 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹. With W1/W0 = 0.75, R = (230/1.667 × 10⁻⁴) × 17 × ln(1.333) = 1.38 × 10⁶ × 17 × 0.2877 = 6.75 × 10⁶ m, about 6750 km.

(c) E = (1/c)(L/D)·ln(W0/W1) = 6000 × 17 × 0.2877 = 29 340 s, about 8.2 hours.

(d) For 5000 km, ln(W0/W1) = Rc/(V·L/D) = 5 × 10⁶ × 1.667 × 10⁻⁴/(230 × 17) = 0.213. The fuel fraction is 1 − e^(−0.213) = 19.2% of the initial cruise weight.

(e) Range is directly proportional to L/D, so a 10% aerodynamic improvement gives 10% more range for the same fuel. Reducing the zero-fuel weight leaves the fuel unchanged but makes the final weight smaller, which raises W0/W1. For example, if the zero-fuel weight falls from 52.5 t to 47.25 t with 17.5 t of fuel, the ratio rises from 1.333 to 1.370 and range increases by about 9.5%. Alternatively, the saving can be taken as extra payload. The Breguet result assumes constant speed, L/D and TSFC, which implies a cruise-climb as weight falls. It also ignores climb, descent, diversion and reserve fuel, winds and engine performance changing with altitude. Real block-fuel planning applies these corrections, and step climbs only approximate the ideal.

questions.q: For a conventional aircraft to be longitudinally statically stable, the centre of gravity must be:
questions.why: A positive static margin, CG ahead of NP, gives dCm/dα < 0 and a restoring pitching moment.

questions.q: Using Lanchester's approximation, the phugoid period of an aircraft flying at 100 m/s is closest to:
Describe the phugoid mode, estimate its period at 120 m/s using Lanchester's approximation, and explain why pilots rarely find it troublesome.
markScheme: Slow oscillation exchanging kinetic and potential energy: height and speed vary at roughly constant angle of attack
Lightly damped (damping linked to drag/L/D), may be neutral or slightly unstable
Long period means pilot (or autopilot) corrects it easily, almost subconsciously; short period mode is more important for handling
questions.modelAnswer: The phugoid is a long-period longitudinal oscillation in which the aircraft trades speed for height and back again, with angle of attack nearly constant. It climbs and slows, then dives and speeds up. Lanchester's approximation gives a period T ≈ π√2·V/g = 4.443 × 120/9.81 ≈ 54 s. Damping comes mainly from drag, so clean aircraft with high L/D have lightly damped phugoids, and some are slightly unstable. Because the motion is so slow, a pilot or autopilot corrects it easily with small control inputs, often without noticing. The fast short-period mode matters much more for handling qualities.

questions.q: Larkspur Aviation is designing a light transport. Preliminary data give: wing–body aerodynamic centre h0 = 0.25c̄, wing–body lift-curve slope a = 5.0/rad, tailplane lift-curve slope at = 3.5/rad, downwash gradient dε/dα = 0.4, and tail volume coefficient V̄H = 0.6. (a) Using hn = h0 + V̄H(at/a)(1 − dε/dα), find the stick-fixed neutral point. (b) With the CG at 0.30c̄, find the static margin and estimate dCm/dα. (c) Find the aft CG limit for a minimum static margin of 5%. (d) Find the neutral point if V̄H is increased to 0.7, and separately if dε/dα rises to 0.5. (e) Discuss what sets the forward CG limit, how fuel burn and loading affect CG, and the case for relaxed stability with fly-by-wire.
markScheme: dCm/dα ≈ −a·Kn = −5.0 × 0.202 ≈ −1.0 per rad (negative, stable)
Aft limit: h = hn − 0.05 = 0.452c̄
V̄H = 0.7: hn = 0.25 + 0.7 × 0.7 × 0.6 = 0.544c̄ (larger tail moves NP aft)
dε/dα = 0.5: hn = 0.25 + 0.6 × 0.7 × 0.5 = 0.46c̄ (more downwash reduces tail effectiveness)
Forward limit: elevator authority to trim at CLmax with flaps/ground effect in the landing flare, stick force per g limits, nose-wheel lift-off at rotation
CG movement: fuel burn (tank positions, swept-wing tanks shift CG), passenger/cargo loading; need loading envelope; very large static margin increases trim drag
Relaxed stability: smaller tail or more aft CG lowers trim drag and weight; requires reliable fly-by-wire augmentation; stick-free NP lies ahead of stick-fixed so margins differ
Sensible conclusion on chosen CG range and sizing
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) hn = 0.25 + 0.6 × (3.5/5.0) × (1 − 0.4) = 0.25 + 0.6 × 0.7 × 0.6 = 0.502c̄.

(b) Kn = 0.502 − 0.30 = 0.202, a static margin of 20% of the mean aerodynamic chord. Approximately, dCm/dα = −a·Kn = −5.0 × 0.202 ≈ −1.0 per radian. It is negative, so the aircraft is statically stable, and quite strongly so.

(c) For a 5% margin, the aft CG limit is 0.502 − 0.05 = 0.452c̄.

(d) With V̄H = 0.7, hn = 0.25 + 0.7 × 0.7 × 0.6 = 0.544c̄. A larger or longer tail moves the neutral point aft and widens the usable CG range. With dε/dα = 0.5, hn = 0.25 + 0.6 × 0.7 × 0.5 = 0.46c̄. More downwash at the tail reduces the tail's change in incidence with α, so the neutral point moves forward. This shows why tail placement relative to the wing wake matters.

(e) The forward CG limit is set by control power rather than stability. With the CG far forward, the elevator must produce a large download to trim. In the landing flare, with flaps down near CLmax and ground effect cutting downwash, it may run out of authority. Rotation at take-off and acceptable stick force per g are further limits. Between the limits, the CG moves as fuel burns, especially in swept wings where tanks lie aft of the root, and with the distribution of passengers and cargo. The design therefore needs a loading envelope, and sometimes fuel management. A large static margin also raises trim drag, because the tail must push down harder. Fly-by-wire lets designers relax stability by moving the CG aft or shrinking the tail, which saves weight and trim drag. The computers then supply artificial stability. This needs highly reliable redundant systems, and the stick-free neutral point, which lies ahead of the stick-fixed one, must still be respected for any reversionary mode. For this transport, a CG range of roughly 0.25–0.45c̄ with a conventional stable layout looks reasonable.

questions.q: Under CS-25 and FAR 25, ultimate load equals limit load multiplied by:
questions.why: A factor of safety of 1.5 applies to limit loads to obtain ultimate loads (CS/FAR 25.303).

questions.q: An airliner fuselage has a radius of 1.95 m and skin thickness 1.8 mm, with a cabin differential pressure of 58 kPa. Calculate the hoop and longitudinal stresses, and explain why fatigue rather than static strength usually governs the skin design.
markScheme: σl = pr/(2t) = 31.4 MPa
Stresses are low compared with alloy strength, but the full cycle is applied every flight, so crack initiation and growth at stress concentrations (windows, doors, fasteners) govern
questions.modelAnswer: The hoop stress is σh = pr/t = 58 000 × 1.95/0.0018 = 62.8 MPa, and the longitudinal stress is half that, 31.4 MPa. These are modest compared with the strength of aluminium alloys of several hundred MPa. But the full pressure cycle is applied once every flight, tens of thousands of times over the aircraft's life. Stress concentrations at windows, doors and fastener holes raise local stresses several-fold, and fatigue cracks can start and grow there. Skin thickness and detail design are therefore set by fatigue life and damage tolerance rather than static strength.

questions.q: A single-cell wing torsion box has a mid-line section of 1.2 m by 0.4 m and a uniform wall thickness of 2.0 mm. It carries a torque of 50 kNm. With G = 27 GPa, find the shear flow, shear stress and rate of twist, and explain why the shear flow is constant around the cell.
markScheme: Enclosed mid-line area A = 1.2 × 0.4 = 0.48 m²
Constant q from longitudinal equilibrium of a wall element with no axial stress gradient in pure torsion
questions.modelAnswer: The mid-line encloses A = 1.2 × 0.4 = 0.48 m². By Bredt–Batho, q = T/(2A) = 50 000/0.96 = 52.1 kN/m, so τ = q/t = 52 100/0.002 = 26.0 MPa. The perimeter is 3.2 m, so ∮ds/t = 1600. The twist rate is dθ/dz = T∮(ds/t)/(4A²G) = 50 000 × 1600/(4 × 0.2304 × 27 × 10⁹) = 3.2 × 10⁻³ rad/m, about 0.18° per metre. In pure torsion there is no axial stress gradient along the box. Axial equilibrium of any small wall element then requires the shear flow entering one edge to equal that leaving the other, so q is constant around a single closed cell.

questions.q: Meridian Aerostructures is preparing the structural design basis for a new airliner with a maximum take-off weight of 150 000 lb (about 68 t). The 1-g stall speed with flaps up is 60 m/s EAS and the wing loading is 6000 N/m². (a) Calculate the positive limit manoeuvring load factor required by CS-25, and the ultimate load factor. (b) Calculate the design manoeuvring speed VA and sketch the positive side of the V–n diagram, labelling its boundaries. (c) For a sharp-edged gust of 10 m/s EAS at VE = 150 m/s with lift-curve slope 5.0/rad, estimate the gust load factor and compare it with the manoeuvre limit. (d) Discuss how fatigue and damage tolerance requirements influence the choice of materials and structural layout, with reference to historical accidents.
markScheme: V–n diagram: stall curve n = (V/Vs)² from origin to VA; horizontal line n = 2.5 to VD; vertical at VD; negative side to −1.0 at VC tapering to 0 at VD
Gust case below 2.5 here (with alleviation factor even lower), but must be checked at all speeds/weights; low wing loading aircraft may be gust-critical

Fatigue: pressurisation and ground–air–ground cycles; Comet 1 (1954) cracks at cut-out corners led to full-scale fatigue testing; Aloha 243 (1988) multiple-site damage led to ageing aircraft programmes

Damage tolerance: crack stoppers/tear straps, multiple load paths, inspectable structure, slow crack growth materials (2024 in tension areas, 7075 in compression), CFRP fatigue-resistant but impact damage and inspection issues
Conclusion linking static, gust and fatigue cases as the design drivers in different regions

The gust case must still be checked across all weights, altitudes and speeds, and for continuous turbulence. Lightly loaded wings with high lift slopes can be gust-critical.

(d) Static loads size much of the wing, but fatigue governs large parts of the airframe, especially the pressurised fuselage and the lower wing skin in tension. The Comet 1 accidents of 1954 showed fatigue cracks growing from stress concentrations at fuselage cut-outs, which led to full-scale fatigue testing and fail-safe design. Aloha Airlines Flight 243 (1988) exposed multiple-site damage in an ageing fuselage and prompted ageing-aircraft inspection programmes. Today's damage-tolerant approach assumes flaws exist, designs for slow crack growth with tear straps and multiple load paths, and sets inspection intervals accordingly. This favours 2024-type alloys where tension and fatigue dominate and 7075-type alloys in compression-critical upper skins. Composites resist fatigue well but are vulnerable to impact damage that may not be visible, so their design allowables and inspection methods differ.
